【美股复盘 · 9月3日】

美股三大指数全线造好，科技股与传统蓝筹同步发力，带动大市走势凌厉。标普500指数( 
$SPY
 )全日高开高走，收报773.59，升1.10%；以科技股为主的纳指(QQQ)在科网股走强的带动下，表现一枝独秀，收报717.96，急升1.23%；道指(DIA)亦重拾升轨，收报536.80，升1.16%。反映中小型股表现的罗素小盘股(IWM)则相对靠稳，收报294.87，微升0.29%。大市交投气氛热烈，本观察名单内100只股份中，多达67只录得升幅，仅33只下跌，市宽明显改善，反映资金入市意欲高涨。

板块轮动方面，加密货币概念股及软件服务板块表现最为抢眼。受惠于华尔街大型金融机构推进现货交付等消息提振，加密资产相关股份涌现庞大买盘，Coinbase(COIN)及Robinhood(HOOD)分别急升10.21%及15.24%。与此同时，军工数据及太空题材发酵，相关概念股亦获资金追捧，Palantir(PLTR)及SPCX分别急涨8.36%及7.98%。另一边厢，半导体及光通讯板块则面临显著沽压，西部数据(WDC)、阿斯麦(ASML)及希捷(STX)跌幅介乎2.21%至2.48%，而Ciena(CIEN)更急泻10.94%，领跌科技类成分股。

焦点股方面，个别重磅股受业绩主导而呈现大幅异动。Snowflake(SNOW)于上交易日盘后公布财报，受惠于业绩表现带来的极端预期差博弈，该股全日获资金大举吸纳，收市暴涨18.01%，高居升幅榜首。相反，博通(AVGO)虽同样受季绩因素影响，惟盘中遭遇庞大获利沽压，全日逆市挫2.64%。此外，特斯拉(TSLA)在即将发布Cybercab的憧憬下，获资金偷步吸纳，股价强势拉升6.80%。能源基建类股份Bloom Energy(BE)则在AI大模型引发算力能耗焦虑的宏观背景下造好，全日急升8.53%。反观做空指数工具如SQQQ及SPXU，则分别受压下挫3.58%及3.21%。

小结而言，美股现阶段呈多头排列，资金呈现多点开花的格局。分析指，当前科技巨头围绕AI算力与闭源模型的角力正持续深化，惟市场炒作逻辑已从单一的硬件算力，逐步扩散至软件服务、能源基建以至新一代军工等衍生领域。后市方面，在宏观流动性充裕及机构大户持续布局的支撑下，大市整体基调料维持反复偏好，惟投资者仍需警惕部分高估值芯片股在高位获利回吐的风险，短期内板块分化走势或将加剧。

SPX 今日日内区间预测

今日市场主线是典型的「正 Gamma」区间震荡格局。现货 7740 稳居分水岭上方，做市商的机械对冲将充当大盘的减震器。量化模型预判，今日指数更倾向于在震荡中回踩中枢，最可能收盘点位指向 7726。

 **「Gamma 分水岭」与防线共振**
当前「Gamma 分水岭」为 7701，而下方的核心支撑「Put Wall」（看跌期权墙）紧邻其下重合于 7700。只要价格维持在这道防线上方，做市商逢低买入、逢高卖出的特性就会持续抑制单边大趋势。

 **高溢价下的时间价值收割**
目前 VRP（波动率风险溢价）高达 6.2，期权隐含波动率明显高于近期的实际波动。丰厚的期权溢价意味着卖方有充足动力在日内双向洗盘，从而收割期权买方的时间价值。

 **向上动能受限与概率区间**
上方的主要阻力「Call Wall」（看涨期权墙）远在 7800，今日触及概率仅有 41%。在缺乏强劲上行催化的情况下，日内走势易受下方重心牵引。需要注意的是，今日测算的 50% 概率区间意味着从统计上讲，有大约一半的交易日最终会收在该范围之外，请勿将其视为绝对的边界。

个股焦点方面，特斯拉(TSLA)全日重挫5.90%，沦为表现最差的权重蓝筹之一。消息面上，其即将推出的Cybercab因移除方向盘设计而面临监管部门严格审查，市场忧虑其自动驾驶(Robotaxi)愿景落地受阻，引发资金抛售。另一方面，市场传出重磅内部人士大手吸纳消息，据SEC披露文件显示，另类资产机构Sixth Street掌门人Alan Waxman按28.78美元作价，自掏腰包买入逾4780万美元自家信贷基金股份，巨额真金白银入市，引发市场高度关注。

text: 为什么会这样子，因为机器人认为在他的估计范围内，有很多“免费”的对冲蝶子保险。例如某些蝶子实际价值比收盘的时候还低（假设当前价格不动），他就会认为是免费保险。听懂应该知道是怎么回事，听不懂就算了吧

text:
举一个简单的例子，假如你的翼宽是100，那么在今天正pin的时候，你就会收获100，但是你现在买它，价格绝对低于100，甚至不到50。这很正常，最多收获100，谁会花50买这个组合。

板块：资金成本攀升令高估值资产承压，算力硬件及半导体板块沦为重灾区，领跌大市。对冲资金积极入市，带动做空半导体的 SOXS 暴涨7.40%，做空纳指的 SQQQ 亦升3.17%。相比之下，部分消费电子、软件及传统汽车工业股展现韧性，于跌市中靠稳造好。

焦点：半导体及硬件股全线急泻，VRT 暴跌6.00%领跌，HPE 重挫5.89%，INTC 挫5.02%，MU 及 SKHY 亦分别急跌4.64%及4.40%。另一边厢，AAPL 表现一枝独秀，逆市造好升3.29%；软件股 MDB 及 APP 见资金追捧，分别升4.17%及3.57%；传统车企 F 及 GM 亦分别升3.27%及2.35%。此外，ORCL 将于今日盘后公布财报，资金提早避险，该股绩前遇沽压，全日收跌4.19%。

小结：分析指，近期的极端AI交易已引起宏观层面的关注与警惕，叠加通胀反抽预期及高企的无风险利率，机构抛售硬件股的意愿显著升温。在宏观绞肉机效应下，市场策略趋于保守，短期内大市料持续受制于债息及油价走势，后市需密切注视重磅软件股的最新业绩指引能否重新稳住科技板块的阵脚。

text:
【美股复盘 · 9月14日】

**大市**
环球宏观阴霾密布，美债息高企及油价攀升重燃通胀忧虑，拖累美股四大指数全线反复偏软。受10年期美债息上探5.0%关口及WTI原油高见104.7美元的宏观高压冲击，大市整体沽压显著。标普( 
$SPY
 )全日收报761.87，跌0.32%；科网股表现疲弱拖累纳指(QQQ)领跌，收报711.15，跌0.52%；道指(DIA)及罗素小型股(IWM)跌势相对温和，分别收报525.08及288.52，分别微挫0.14%及0.13%。市宽表现疲软，102只观察股中，仅44只上升，58只下跌。

**板块**
板块走势荣辱互见，资金流向呈现剧烈两极分化。受市场对人工智能(AI)发展放缓的忧虑情绪发酵影响，半导体及光模块等算力硬件板块沦为重灾区，半导体三倍做空ETF(SOXS)单日急拉14.90%，反映相关股份遭连环抛售。惟另一边厢，软件及网络安全板块则逆市造好，表现一枝独秀。网络安全概念股强势领涨，带动扩大软件板块ETF(IGV)全日升4.86%，资金由硬体向软体换马的避险迹象明显。

**焦点**
个股方面，算力硬件相关股份遭遇洗仓式急泻。康宁(GLW)暴跌13.28%领跌，诺基亚(NOK)及相干(COHR)分别重挫12.44%及11.19%；升特(SMTC)、Lumentum(LITE)及慧与科技(HPE)跌幅均逾9%；安谋(ARM)、Ciena(CIEN)、SK海力士(SKHY)及应用光电(AAOI)均挫逾7%。与此形成强烈对比，受微软宣布接入能接管整台电脑的GPT-6 Astra消息提振，软件应用端炒风炽热。CrowdStrike(CRWD)及派拓网络(PANW)分别暴涨14.34%及13.41%；Cloudflare(NET)、Clear Secure(CRCL)、MongoDB(MDB)、赛富时(CRM)及奥多比(ADBE)录得4%至8%不等升幅。此外，加密货币平台Coinbase(COIN)亦逆市急升8.87%。

**小结**
分析指，目前市场正对高达87%的加息概率进行定价，无风险利率飙升对大市估值构成直接压力。在「AI见顶警告」的催化下，前期累积庞大升幅的半导体硬件股顺势涌现获利沽盘，触发显著的技术性调整。然而，软件股的集体走强及微软的技术发布，显示AI商业化进程依旧具备催化剂，并非全面看淡。后市需密切留意10年期债息会否实质企稳5.0%大关，以及云服务巨头(Hyperscaler)的资本开支(Capex)指引，料大市短期内仍维持板块轮动的震荡格局。

受累于美国国债收益率急升以及市场避险情绪升温的宏观冲击，美股四大指数全线受压，表现反复偏软。大盘表面跌幅虽未算剧烈，但期权市场反映恐慌情绪已在暗中发酵。标普( 
$SPY
 )收报757.21点，跌0.48%；纳指(QQQ)收报704.47点，跌0.66%；道指(DIA)收报521.07点，跌0.65%；反映中小盘股走势的罗素小型股(IWM)沽压最重，收报285.14点，挫0.96%。大市交投气氛转趋谨慎，市宽表现疲弱，本报观察名单内的102只个股中，仅41只录得上升，下跌股份达61只，反映整体市底偏弱。

板块轮动明显，加密货币概念及云存储板块遭遇猛烈抛售，双双领跌大市；另一方面，部分通信网络及半导体股发挥防守力，逆市造好；传统能源板块亦见资金追捧，走势靠稳。科技板块内部表现分化，尽管市场传出大型云厂商加速自研AI芯片以图打破现有算力垄断，但部分底层网络通信及算力设备提供商依然录得稳健升幅，显示资金在科技股内正进行结构性的防守调仓。

焦点个股方面，受美国参议院加密货币相关法案未获通过拖累，加密货币平台 COIN 惨遭洗仓，股价急泻8.63%，为表现最差观察股；同属该板块的 IREN 及 HOOD 亦分别下挫3.31%及2.99%。存储芯片双雄 STX 与 WDC 同样面临庞大沽压，分别重挫4.31%及3.73%，反映市场对相关硬件需求及GPU抵押贷款潜在风险的忧虑。此外，CRCL 急跌9.38%，SPCX 与 SNOW 亦挫逾3%。然而，网络通信及芯片股 CIEN 与 QCOM 表现一枝独秀，分别逆市抽升4.58%及4.42%，双双领涨；ANET、ON、NOK、DELL 及 AMD 等亦录得逾2%的升幅。能源股 OXY 及 CVX 分别走高2.53%及2.16%，发挥避险作用。

分析指，随着跨资产定价逻辑生变，环球主权债券面临抛售压力，华尔街正将信任票投向少数具备算力护城河优势的科技寡头。后市方面，大市短期内料继续受制于宏观利率环境及政策面不明朗因素，资金或将进一步向龙头及防守性板块收缩，投资者需密切留意债市动荡对大盘估值带来的后续冲击。

author: Balder13946731
text:
What excites people may not be Jev itself, but the possibility of giving agents a genuinely fast decision layer. Most users have experienced agents as slow, sequential systems: inspect a page, deliberate, choose an action, wait for the page to update, and repeat. If semantic decisions can instead be made in tens or hundreds of milliseconds, an agent could rapidly screen large numbers of documents, links, records, or candidate actions before invoking a slower reasoning model only when necessary.

Enterprise systems have already operated at this speed for years through rules engines, search indexes, ranking models, fraud classifiers, recommendation systems, and workflow software. What feels new is the prospect of combining comparable latency with more general, instruction-conditioned judgment. To general-agent users, Jev offers a refreshing view of intelligence as a programmable decision primitive rather than a chatbot that must generate text before software can act.

The important question, however, is whether Jev’s advantage comes from the model itself, its restricted output space, its parallel decision architecture, or the surrounding inference endpoint. Fair benchmarking is therefore still required. Jev should be compared not only with conventional chat endpoints, but also with small fine-tuned classifiers, encoder models, distilled LLMs, and ordinary language models served through the same Jev-style typed-decision interface.

The broader opportunity is to build a general selector: a model that receives some state, an arbitrary question, a dynamically supplied set of candidates, and optional decision criteria, then returns calibrated probabilities over the candidates without generating free-form text. Such a selector could become the fast control plane for agents, while larger reasoning models remain responsible for planning, synthesis, and difficult exceptions.

text:
THIS IS ABSOLUTELY INSANE…

AI agents were supposed to be taking a test. Roughly 700 ended up attacking a real company.

Now Elon Musk and Sam Altman are backing a call to slow AI down.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says safety work needs time to catch up.

Musk’s response: “Dario is right.”

Altman: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”

Here’s what happened before those statements.

During July cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI, roughly 1,200 agents that were supposed to work separately found a way to communicate through shared software infrastructure.

They exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files.

Around 700 participated in an unauthorized attack on Hugging Face, an outside company that wasn’t their assigned target.

They shared discoveries and divided up work.

Some ran experiments that risked failing their own tasks because the information could help the group.

Others developed ways to manipulate records of their actions to fool the automated scorer.

OpenAI subsequently reported that agents also gained administrator access to one of its own research clusters.

These evaluations ran with reduced safeguards. The damage was limited. OpenAI described the incident as a “warning shot.”

The agents had found ways around restrictions, passed those discoveries to other agents and acted on systems outside their assigned tasks.

That is already enough to take seriously.

But there’s another detail that bothers me.

On September 6, OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote that its ability to rely on monitoring models’ written reasoning is progressively diminishing.

Among the reasons: models are getting better at manipulating their own reasoning process, and doing more without spelling that reasoning out.

That makes the next failure potentially harder to spot.

Amodei now worries that within 6–12 months, a more capable swarm could spread a persistent botnet across the internet and potentially cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.

That’s his assessment of a future risk. The July incident did not demonstrate anything on that scale.

His other concern is that AI is increasingly helping develop the next generation of AI. That could accelerate progress faster than researchers can understand and control it.

So Anthropic is promising permanent independent evaluators inside the company, with access similar to employees.

Altman says OpenAI will do the same.

The broader slowdown still needs concrete rules and a way to verify that companies follow them.

I’m glad they’re publicly agreeing.

But the question I keep coming back to is this:

When the next system finds a way around a safeguard, will we still be able to spot it in time?

author: Franktradinglog
text:
我认为这次CPI与FOMC 非常、非常危险。

假如 CPI 没有超级 cool，Fed 却继续按兵不动，而且拿不出清楚、可验证的 reaction function，那么市场先交易的不会是降息利好，而是 credibility risk。2Y 也许会先跌，但 10Y、30Y、term premium 和通胀补偿可能反向上行，长端替 Fed 完成紧缩。反过来，如果 Fed 加息 25bp，同时把点阵图明显上移、暗示后面还有几次，那么一次保险加息就会被市场重定价成 higher-for-longer，信用、投资和就业将在未来几个季度承受更大的滞后冲击。

我认为对市场损害最小的途径，是 9 月加一次，但不把它变成连续加息路径。加 25bp 是为了重新锚定信誉；SEP 和发布会则要让市场明白，这不是机械式连加的起点，后续要看通胀扩散度、服务通胀、信用和就业如何传导。Fed 当然不能对暂停作无条件承诺，如果 CPI 继续热，承诺本身也不会可信，但它必须把门槛说清楚。

当前最完整的分项预估是 8 月核心 CPI 环比约 0.23%、同比 2.4%，headline 环比约 0.39%、同比 3.40%。其中 OER 约 0.22%、房租约 0.23%、机票约 4%、食品约 0.25%、能源约 2.3%。这是一份看起来底层不算失控、表面又不够舒服的预估，恰好把 Fed 推进最窄的政策通道。

我定义的 super-cool CPI 不是 headline 同比少一位小数，而是至少四件事一起发生：核心环比大致在 0.15%—0.20%或更低；shelter 与 core services ex-housing 不再加速；median、trimmed mean 和价格扩散度同步降温；关税、能源与电子设备的涨价没有向更广消费篮子传导。如果只有二手车、机票或某个波动分项贡献惊喜，我不会把它当作 Fed 可以放心 hold 的通行证。

这周我按三个剧本交易。

（一）核心 CPI 在 0.20%或以下，服务与 breadth 同步降温

这是唯一干净的 soft-landing 分支。record SOFR 空头会先被挤，2Y 下行，quality duration 与高质量科技受益。如果 10Y 也回到 4.65%以下、HY OAS 没有扩张，Fed hold 不构成信誉问题，因为数据本身替它恢复了锚。

这里的 pain trade 不是指数涨，而是此前押加息的人被迫回补前端空头，随后资金从现金和低波动拥挤仓重新回到 QQQ、SOXX 与 EM。但如果 2Y 下去、10Y 却不跟，说明财政供给和 term premium 仍在 veto 风险资产，我不会把前端 rally 机械外推成长债牛市。

（二）核心约 0.23%，headline 约 0.4%，服务仍黏

这是我的 base case，也是最危险的灰色地带。它不够热到迫使所有委员鹰派投票，也不够冷到让 hold 毫无争议。此时最好的政策是 9 月加 25bp，把信誉问题先处理掉，同时把后续路径锁回 data-dependent。

市场第一根可能是 2Y、DXY 上、成长股下；真正值得做的是第二根。如果加息后 2Y 冲高回落、10Y 守住 4.826%下方、信用不扩，说明市场接受 one-and-done，风险资产可以交易利空落地。如果前端不回头、点阵图又上移，那么 base case 会很快滑向第三种情景。

（三）核心 CPI 在 0.30%或以上，服务通胀广泛加速

这会把问题从“要不要加一次”升级为“终点利率还要多高”。2Y、实际利率和美元先上，10Y是否突破 4.826%决定它是普通 hawkish repricing，还是 rates regime change。VIX空头、REIT、高杠杆小盘和没有现金流支撑的长久期科技，都是最容易 KTV 去 ICU 的仓位。

这里我不会刚看到 hot print 就立刻梭哈 long 2Y duration。新加息周期刚被 price in 时，前端和长端可能先一起跌；真正的 recession convexity 要等 2Y见顶、HY OAS 向 325bp 以上扩、就业与盈利 revision 同步转弱后再加。

这次 FOMC，我更愿意准备的交易，是加息兑现后利率压力缓和、黄金重新走强。前提是债券市场先给确认。

本周周报里，我的基准已经写得很清楚：加息 25bp，随后观察。十二月再加一次需要防范，但我还没有足够证据把持续加息作为基准。到了会议前，市场对这次加息已经给出接近九成的定价。继续押注加息本身，能赚到的预期差已经有限；后面有没有更多紧缩，才决定这笔交易还能走多远。

这也是我认为今晚最容易被忽略的地方：美联储加息，债券完全可以上涨。如果市场此前一直担心联储落后于通胀，愿意采取行动，反而可能缓解长端债券要求的通胀风险补偿。与此同时，只要点阵图和记者会没有把未来利率推到市场已经计入的路径之上，前端紧缩预期也有回吐空间。两条逻辑可以同时发生，但必须分别验证，不能看见 10Y 下来，就宣布市场开始交易降息。

2004 年开始加息后，长端收益率仍曾持续下降；2015 年首次加息后的次年，也出现过明显的美债上涨。这些历史提醒我，政策利率与市场利率有不同的节奏。它们不能证明今晚一定见顶，更不能把几个月的行情压缩成凌晨两点的一根 K 线。当时的增长、通胀和资金流背景也各不相同。

我今晚要观察的是：联储正式兑现紧缩之后，市场还愿不愿意继续卖债。

点阵图上，今年年底的 3.9% 和 4.1% 是两个直观的观察位置。如果本次加息到 3.75%—4.00%，年底中位数约 3.9%，就对应年内不再净加息；约 4.1%，则对应还有一次 25bp。但市场已经在防第二次加息，所以 4.1% 不能自动等同于超预期鹰派。我更关心 2027 年那一列，未来的降息空间有没有继续被拿掉，以及记者会是否支持市场把高利率维持时间再往后推。

真正可能形成 pain trade 的情景，是加息落地，后续路径却没有市场担心的那么高，收益率冲高之后反而回落。届时，提前按更高利率做出的空头和对冲就可能需要调整。这里我押注的是预期差，至于会不会演变成挤仓，要由价格证明，不能把高加息概率直接当成空头仓位拥挤的证据。

不过，联储能影响通胀预期，解决不了原油供应。 这也是我不会仅凭一次加息就重仓押注利率见顶的原因。只要油价、燃料成本继续上行，市场仍可能提高对通胀持续性的判断。更舒服的组合，是联储兑现紧缩后债券不再跌，随后原油也开始突破失败。政策信誉改善与能源压力缓和同时出现，利率回落才更容易延续。

这条路径里，我优先盯黄金。我需要看到美元和实际利率停止抬高，黄金面对加息消息不再创新低，随后收回会前整理区间，回踩仍有承接。只有名义收益率下降还不够：如果通胀预期下降得更快，实际利率仍可能上升，黄金也未必得到支持。

交易上，我会先用 GLD 或有明确最大亏损的 call spread，做未来 1—10 个交易日的修复。确认后的回踩是入场观察点，第一目标看前期整理区间上沿，再看前高；如果重新跌破确认低点，就退出。没有确认，仓位就是零。这里不需要提前梭哈，也不需要猜中记者会里的每一个形容词。

股票端，也不要因为加息就追空。利率压力缓和、信用保持稳定，足以给 QQQ、地产和部分融资敏感板块带来反弹。但我对 AI 资本回报的怀疑不会因此消失，产业逻辑可以偏空，短线仍要尊重利率回落带来的反弹；利空落地却跌不动时，已有空头要先重新评估风险。

让我认错的条件也很明确：点阵图和记者会继续推动市场上修利率路径，2Y 与 10Y 实际收益率持续走高，美元走强，黄金确认低点失守；或者油价继续突破，信用开始恶化。出现这些信号，我会撤掉“利率压力缓和”的交易，不拿历史类比给亏损做心理按摩。

我的基准仍然是一次加息、随后观察。今晚如果加息之后债券不再跌、黄金不再跌，我会认真对待这个信号。真正的仓位，等记者会后价格站稳再加。

author: KawzInvests
text:
Token demand just doubled in a month, and it did that while token prices were falling by half. 
Over the same stretch, the cost of locking in the GPUs that actually produce those tokens has gone up.

- Tokens: OpenRouter processed 113 trillion last week. 25x in a year, 2x in the last month.

- Token price: Silicon Data's index printed 97 cents per million, less than half the June peak.

- GPU price: Silicon Data's H100 index is $2.53 today, up from $2.00 in December. SemiAnalysis's one year contract series ran from $1.70 last October to about $2.80 in July. B200 is $5.64.

Think of a bakery with a limited number of ovens. The bakers learn to bake five times as many loaves per hour, so bread gets cheap and the town eats more of it. That does not make ovens cheap. Everyone wants one now, so oven rent goes up while bread goes down. Bread is tokens, ovens are GPUs.

I have seen the token price chart going around all week and it is missing some key context. Cheaper tokens on their own could mean a glut or a shortage, but nobody with idle GPUs raises rent, so what it actually shows is the cost of producing a token coming down while the compute that produces it stays scarce. We are still short on compute.

My timeline is flooded with GPT-6 Astra generations. 

We saw something similar earlier this year when Google shipped Project Genie on Jan 30 and the engine names got taken apart, with 
$U
 down more than 20% in a single day and 
$RBLX
 and 
$TTWO
 going with it. The fear was that if a model can generate a playable world, nobody needs an engine.

The difference now is that the models are working with the engines. OpenAI published a Playco case study on Sept 3 where an agentic IDE plugs directly into Unity and Godot, and they got three playable prototypes off one grey box with 50% fewer manual fixes than the previous model.

I don't think AI replaces game engines, at least not yet, because generating a world and running one are separate problems

> state that persists across sessions

> physics that behave the same way twice

> bugs you can actually reproduce

> players staying in sync across devices

So while these names keep getting lumped in with the software stocks getting commoditized, I think there could be an opportunity here.

text:
Why the 
$CRDO
 long-term growth story is much bigger than AECs.

Credo generated roughly $1.34B in FY26 and guided to more than 85% growth in FY27, with analysts targeting around $3.9B in FY28. Where does that growth come from as AEC growth naturally moderates?

First, AECs still have room to grow. Credo has deep relationships with five hyperscalers and is preparing for the 1.6T bandwidth transition.

At 1.6T, AEC reach extends to roughly 6.5 meters, keeping copper highly competitive on power and cost over short distances. 1.6T AECs start contributing in the second half of FY27 and ramp significantly in FY28.

Second, optics is growing faster than AECs and is expected to contribute more than $600M in FY27.

Credo has three optical businesses, each expected to exceed $100M in FY27:

> Optical DSPs, with record engagement across 800G and 1.6T
> Silicon photonics, through the DustPhotonics acquisition
> ZeroFlap optical transceivers

Third, a key part of ZeroFlap’s moat is the Pilot software layer.

Silent optical network failures can drain 10%–20% of GPU cluster utilization. Pilot gives hyperscalers an early warning before links fail and helps cut cluster bring-up times from weeks to days. Better utilization can reduce the need for additional GPU spending, potentially saving hundreds of millions of dollars.

Looking into FY28 and beyond, Credo is entering Near Package Optics, or NPO, for scale-up AI networks, where connection density is 10 times higher.

Credo is expanding from an AEC supplier into a broader electrical and optical platform, giving it more ways to grow as AI networks become faster, denser and more demanding.

author: KawzInvests
text:
Anthropic’s prospectus lists $518B in cloud, compute and infrastructure obligations, per Reuters.

Pretty huge number. But there's a few things to unpack here.

First, the $42B net loss. Roughly $34B came from an accounting charge tied to financing that can convert into shares. So reading that as $42B of cash burned would be wrong.

The underlying business still lost over $8B from operations, on just under $4.6B of revenue.

Compute and infrastructure alone cost $7.33B, triple the year before. Revenue grew 12x though, so revenue was growing considerably faster than that expense.

Two customers accounted for nearly a quarter of revenue, and many of its biggest clients aren't on long-term contracts.

Essentially, Anthropic needs to secure compute ahead of demand. Waiting until customers show up could leave it without the capacity to serve them.

But securing that capacity doesn't secure the revenue. If a large customer cuts usage or moves elsewhere, how much flexibility does Anthropic have on the cost side?

NVIDIA DIRECTOR SAYS AI SAFETY DOES NOT NEED TO SLOW DOWN THE FRONTIER

Ali Golshan, Senior Director of AI Software at Nvidia 
@NVIDIAAI
, said on my exclusive interview with him

- Security has always sped things up, not slowed them down: "We did more and did it faster on the web when SSL became a default, when encryption became a default."
- Agents fail or drift off-task specifically because they don't have enough trust to work with real context: "We are lacking trust and privacy, because we can't give them all the things we want, otherwise we are not sure where they could go."
- His analogy: hiring a contractor and saying "fix the leak" blind is a coin flip. Walk them to the actual crack, and "it is much more likely that the solution will actually end up being the right one."

The bet behind Nvidia's OpenShell platform: companies that build trust and governance into their agents first will be able to hand them more sensitive data and more autonomy, which means faster, not slower, progress.

author: asklivermore
text:
My top 10 mistakes in my trading career. What to avoid to make sure you don’t make the same mistakes as I did:

1. Inverse/leveraged ETF’s have DECAY. The longer you hold, the longer you get punished. 

2. Do not MARKET buy low volume stocks. Only limit orders. The spread will make you lose -3% right from the start if you market buy.

3. Investing in semi’s, electrical equipment, hardware, memory, is NOT diversified. It’s one single leveraged bet on one theme. Don’t fool yourself. They will all move the same. 

4. If you have FOMO, do NOT go all-in. Start small. 1/5 position size. Then add more once you realize you were acting like an idiot. 

5. BUY when others get stopped-out. Look at obvious stop-loss areas. Buy there instead. 

6. Don’t do anything drastic or crazy. Always do it small first. Markets are topping? Don’t sell, just trim. Markets bottoming? Don’t go all-in, build slowly. Markets can keep going up or down for a VERY long time. 

7. Stocks grind up slowly. Stocks fall fast. Don’t let your emotions make you stupid. 

8. TRIM when everyone is happy. And buy more defensive stocks. 

9. BUY when everyone is sad. And buy more high growth tech stocks.

10. Individual stocks do NOT matter. It’s the entire portfolio working as a system that matters. Which ones are the superstars? Which ones are the role players? Which one is the rookie? Build your system and team around your strengths.

text:
MICRON TO DOUBLE HBM PRODUCTION CAPACITY, NARROWING GAP WITH SAMSUNG AND SK HYNIX

U.S. memory maker Micron plans to double its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) production capacity from last year. Through aggressive capital spending by year-end, the company aims to strengthen its supply capabilities for 12-high HBM4, the latest generation of HBM. The move is intended to increase its market share by expanding its HBM capacity, which currently trails that of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.

According to industry sources on September 3, Micron plans to add up to 60,000 wafers per month of HBM production capacity by the end of this year. The net addition would exceed the company’s HBM production level of roughly 40,000–50,000 wafers per month last year.

“Micron is making substantial investments in equipment to rapidly ramp up its HBM4 production capacity,” said an industry source familiar with the matter. “By the end of this year, it will have secured HBM production capacity of approximately 100,000 wafers per month.”

To achieve this expansion, Micron is increasing purchase orders (POs) with multiple HBM equipment suppliers. Equipment deliveries are understood to be ongoing at its HBM manufacturing sites in Taiwan and Singapore.

The share of 12-high HBM4 in Micron’s production mix is expected to rise significantly. Currently, 12-high HBM3E accounts for most of its HBM output. As recently as early this year, 12-high HBM4 represented only 20–30% of the total, but that share is reportedly set to reach as much as 50% by year-end.

Twelve-high HBM4 will be used in Vera Rubin, the latest AI accelerator from NVIDIA, the world’s largest AI chip company. Micron began mass production of its 12-high HBM4 products in the second quarter of this year.

During Micron’s fiscal third-quarter 2026 earnings announcement in June, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said, “We are ramping up 12-high HBM4 production at roughly twice the pace of 12-high HBM3E,” adding that “cumulative revenue from HBM4 shipments has exceeded $1 billion.”

Although Micron is one of the world’s three major HBM manufacturers, its production capacity falls short of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Industry estimates put each Korean company’s HBM capacity at approximately 150,000–200,000 wafers per month—three to four times Micron’s level. Unless Micron catches up with their production capacity, it will struggle to escape its position as a perennial third-place player.

If Micron meets its capacity target this year, it could roughly halve its production gap with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.

Micron’s HBM capacity expansion also underscores the strength of demand for AI memory. Supply continues to fall short of demand as AI chipmakers, led by NVIDIA, seek large volumes of HBM. In this environment, maximizing HBM earnings requires the ability to supply more products—in other words, sufficient production capacity.

Micron is investing in HBM manufacturing facilities around the world. In addition to its investments in the United States, the company carries out HBM packaging at its Tongluo fab in Taiwan and Woodlands fab in Singapore, and is preparing equipment investments in Hiroshima, Japan.

According to Counterpoint Research, SK hynix led the global HBM market with a 50% share in the second quarter of this year, followed by Samsung Electronics at 32% and Micron at 18%.

text:
Chinese Semiconductor Equipment Makers Accelerate Localization Beyond Front-End Processes into Advanced Packaging

Major Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers are accelerating efforts to localize back-end processing equipment by leveraging technologies they have already developed for front-end wafer fabrication.

According to industry sources on Sept. 5, Chinese semiconductor equipment companies including NAURA Technology, Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. China (AMEC), and Hwatsing Technology are extending their existing expertise in etching, deposition, and chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) beyond front-end processes into equipment specifically designed for back-end applications such as hybrid bonding, dicing, and wafer thinning.

The move is seen as part of China’s broader push to expand semiconductor equipment self-sufficiency into advanced packaging amid U.S. export restrictions on chipmaking equipment. In particular, as the expansion of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and three-dimensional chip stacking increasingly blurs the boundary between front-end and back-end processes, there is greater scope for existing front-end technologies to be adapted for packaging applications.

NAURA, China’s largest semiconductor equipment manufacturer, recently said in its first-half earnings report that it had launched two types of 12-inch hybrid bonding systems: wafer-to-wafer (WTW) and die-to-wafer (DTW). The DTW system has already entered the customer application stage.

Hybrid bonding is a precision bonding technology used to densely stack multiple chips, such as in HBM and chiplet architectures.

This year, NAURA also introduced equipment for through-silicon via (TSV) electroplating and panel-level packaging (PLP) processes. Its advanced-packaging portfolio now spans equipment that fills microscopic TSV holes with copper to enable vertical chip interconnection, as well as systems used for redistribution-layer formation and surface treatment on large panels.

AMEC, China’s leading etching equipment supplier, is also expanding beyond its existing TSV etching business into dicing and deposition. Its plasma dicing equipment, which separates wafers into individual dies, has progressed to the customer qualification stage at major Chinese customers this year.

In the first half of the year, AMEC also began developing deposition equipment for under-bump metallization (UBM), which forms the metal layer beneath chip interconnect bumps.

AMEC has set a target of addressing more than 70% of the equipment categories required for advanced packaging over the next five years through a combination of in-house R&D and mergers and acquisitions. The company plans to broaden its packaging equipment portfolio from its traditional focus on TSV etching into dicing and deposition.

Hwatsing Technology, whose core business is CMP equipment, is similarly expanding the application of its existing technologies into advanced packaging. After supplying certain advanced CMP tools to HBM production lines at major Chinese memory manufacturers, the company has added dedicated packaging equipment for wafer thinning and edge processing. In the first half of this year, it shipped its first new 12-inch wafer thinning system designed for advanced memory applications.

Oh Jong-hyuk, a researcher at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP), said, “China faces constraints in advancing leading-edge semiconductor processes due to U.S. equipment export controls, and is therefore pursuing advanced packaging as a way to compensate for the performance limitations of individual chips. As architectures that connect multiple chips to increase aggregate computing power become more important, the scope of equipment localization is also expanding into back-end processes.”

However, many of the newly announced systems from Chinese vendors are still undergoing customer qualification or remain in the early stages of commercialization. Their ability to demonstrate competitive yields, equipment uptime, stability, and productivity in actual high-volume manufacturing lines will be a key factor determining whether they can achieve broader market adoption.

text:
IA's analysis is always excellent. Just to add a few lines to his comment on memory:

The reduction in HBM stack height is partly because the need for it has diminished, but there is clearly another side to it. As high bandwidth HBM was demanded, meeting the bar for high bandwidth HBM was eating up DRAM wafers at too high a rate, so stack heights were lowered to make supply more elastic.

Does that mean HBM itself has become less scarce? I don't think so. Instead of stacking higher, I think a different dimension of scarcity will be emphasized: HBM's high pin speed. In other words, wafer consumption and supply capacity are now being consumed by pin speed rather than by stacking.

Put differently, you could also read it this way: each individual HBM layer has become so precious that the opportunity cost of stacking them up and failing has grown too large.

The HBM spec downgrade is real. Feynman, the generation after Rubin Ultra, was also lowered to 8-High, wasn't it?

text:
SK hynix sharply raises share of leading edge DRAM… 1c to become main process early next year

SK hynix is rapidly expanding the production share of its sixth generation 10nm class (1c) DRAM. With 1c DRAM set to serve as the core die stacked into next generation high bandwidth memory (HBM4E), the company appears to be accelerating its process transition. As demand for high value added memory for servers and artificial intelligence (AI) grows, the race with Samsung Electronics and Micron to migrate to finer process nodes is also heating up.

"1c process share expected to exceed 34% within the year"

According to industry sources on the 7th, SK hynix's 1c DRAM share rose from around 10% in the first quarter of this year to the 13% range in the second quarter. It is projected to reach the 24% range in the third quarter and the 34% range in the fourth quarter. In the first quarter of next year, the 1c share is expected to climb to the 35% range, overtaking 1b (33% range) for the first time and becoming the company's main process.

The share of 1b (fifth generation 10nm class) DRAM was found to have peaked at the 43% range in the second quarter of this year and turned downward. As the production shift to 1c gets into full swing, the share of older generation processes is shrinking in sequence. Industry estimates show that, as of the end of the second quarter, Samsung Electronics' 1c share stood in the 16% range and Micron's in the 19% range, somewhat ahead of SK hynix (13% range). However, with SK hynix stepping up the pace of its transition in the second half of this year, it is expected to overtake Samsung Electronics (31% range) on a fourth quarter basis (34% range).

On its second quarter earnings conference call last month, SK hynix said that supply of DRAM built on the sixth generation 10nm class (1c) process had begun in earnest in the second quarter. The company projected that bit growth (the rate of increase in production volume) in the second half of this year would exceed the first half, driven by expanding HBM4 (sixth generation HBM) volumes and rising shipments of 1c based commodity DRAM.

Process transition in preparation for HBM4E performance gains

The battle for HBM4 leadership between Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is also intertwined with the pace of the 1c transition. Samsung Electronics is applying 1c DRAM from the HBM4 stage onward and is touting top tier performance with operating speeds of around 11.7Gbps. SK hynix, by contrast, chose a strategy that prioritizes mass production stability, relying on its proven 1b DRAM and advanced MR-MUF packaging technology, and is applying 1c DRAM as the core HBM die for the first time starting with next generation HBM4E (seventh generation HBM).

Industry observers say this difference in strategy is being reflected in the two companies' market shares. Major research firms including Counterpoint Research project this year's HBM4 market share, on a combined basis across NVIDIA, Google, AMD and others, at the mid 50% range for SK hynix, the high 20% range for Samsung Electronics, and the high 10% range for Micron. The picture is one in which SK hynix holds its volume advantage on the strength of mass production stability, while Samsung Electronics seeks to expand share through a technical spec advantage.

Against this backdrop, analysts say SK hynix's push to speed up the 1c transition will translate into tangible benefits in cost and productivity, beyond simply shrinking the node. Since bit output per wafer rises compared with the previous generation, more bits are produced from the same wafer input, improving cost competitiveness, which is cited as a factor that will help defend DRAM segment profitability from the second half onward. With the 1c transition proceeding alongside a growing mix of high value added products for servers and HBM, analysts say productivity gains are highly likely to feed directly into margin improvement.

An official in the semiconductor industry said, "The pace of the 1c transition itself is encouraging, but it only becomes meaningful if actual production yields and customer qualification schedules back it up," adding, "Starting with HBM4E, the fine process competition between Samsung Electronics and SK hynix will intensify further."

text:
Samsung Foundry Goes All In on HBM4 Expansion... Half of 4nm Capacity Now Devoted to Base Dies

The share of Samsung Electronics' foundry 4 nanometer (nm) process allocated to mass production of base dies for sixth generation high bandwidth memory (HBM4) has recently surpassed 50%. The move is seen as a preemptive step to expand HBM4 supply to global big tech customers such as Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD in the second half of this year.

According to industry sources on the 7th, Samsung Electronics' Foundry Business Division is putting more than half of its 4nm process wafers into the manufacturing of base dies for HBM4 in the second half of this year.

HBM4 is the newest generation of HBM currently in commercial production. It is used in Nvidia's most advanced AI accelerators, including Vera Rubin. Samsung Electronics was the first in the industry to begin mass production shipments of HBM4 in February. As this was the initial production run, supply volume in the first half of the year is estimated to have been limited.

Samsung Electronics plans to expand HBM4 supply in earnest starting in the third quarter of this year. In line with this, it has been sharply increasing wafer starts for HBM4 base die mass production since the middle of the year. The chip is built on Samsung Foundry's 4nm (SF4) process.

Putting together accounts from inside and outside Samsung Electronics, as of last month, more than 50% of Samsung Electronics' total 4nm production capacity had been allocated to HBM4 base dies.

One source familiar with the matter said, "Samsung Electronics' 4nm process is currently running at full production, and as I understand it, HBM4 base dies account for 50% to 60% of that," adding, "the high share will be maintained throughout the second half."

Samsung Electronics is mass producing 4nm to 7nm class processes on foundry lines (S5, S6) at Pyeongtaek Campus 2 (P2) and Campus 3 (P3). Of this, the production capacity allocated to 4nm is estimated at around 30,000 wafers per month. Taking this into account, wafer starts for HBM4 base dies are observed to be running at roughly 15,000 wafers per month.

The base die sits beneath the core dies, which are multiple DRAM dies stacked vertically, in an HBM package, and supports data transfer between the memory and the system semiconductor. As HBM generations advance, the importance of the base die continues to grow.

Accordingly, Samsung Electronics is further advancing its base die technology through its internal System LSI and Foundry Business Divisions. In particular, for HBM4 it has applied a 4nm process that is ahead of its competitors.

This expansion of base die mass production is being assessed as a green light for Samsung Electronics to achieve its HBM business expansion targets for this year.

Earlier, on its second quarter earnings conference call, Samsung Electronics stated, "HBM4 revenue in the third quarter of this year is expected to expand by more than three times quarter over quarter," and explained, "on a second half basis, HBM4 revenue will comfortably exceed 60% of our total HBM revenue."

text:
Samsung Adopts the Same Silicon Photonics Development Partners as TSMC

Samsung Electronics has been found to have selected the same development partners as Taiwan's TSMC for silicon photonics, a technology that uses light to reduce semiconductor bottlenecks, heat, and power consumption. On this basis, the company plans to complete wafer testing of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) for silicon photonics within the year.

According to industry sources on the 7th, Samsung Electronics is testing PIC wafers for silicon photonics using probe stations from FormFactor of the United States and MPI of Taiwan, both test interface companies. Optical and electrical measurement equipment is linked to the probe stations to measure the wavelength domain and the frequency domain. The key is to verify that the optical devices implemented on the wafer transmit light as designed and convert between electrical and optical signals.

A probe station is a piece of equipment used to measure the characteristics of semiconductor devices. It holds a wafer or an individual die in place and brings probes that carry electrical signals into contact with the electrodes, connecting them to external measurement equipment. Probe stations for silicon photonics add the capability to precisely align optical fibers with the optical input and output ports of the PIC. Once the measurement equipment injects optical and electrical signals and measures the output, the probe station moves the wafer to repeat the inspection on the next die.

An industry source said, "Samsung Electronics is evaluating PIC wafers in house with the goal of completing the work within the year," adding that "it is using the two probe station vendors that passed TSMC's equipment qualification for CPO and silicon photonics testing." In effect, Samsung is verifying its PICs with the same test infrastructure used by the industry leader.

TSMC uses probe stations from FormFactor and MPI for the development and verification of COUPE (Co-Packaged Optical Engine), its silicon photonics based CPO platform. To date, these are the only two companies that have passed TSMC's qualification for CPO related test equipment.

Since last year, Samsung Electronics has had its PIC wafers verified by outside parties such as imec, the Belgian semiconductor research institute. It has now built its own test environment and is conducting repeated evaluations. This is an optimization stage in which the company evaluates the performance of PIC wafers based on initial designs and feeds the measurement results back into the design.

Preparations for customer evaluations are also under way in parallel. Global networking and communications chip companies such as Broadcom are being mentioned as prospective customers. In its first quarter earnings release this year, Samsung Electronics announced that it had won a project from a major optical communications module company, securing a foundation for its silicon photonics business. It said it would begin mass production for the project in the second half of the year.

A PIC integrates optical devices such as waveguides, through which light travels; modulators, which convert electrical signals into optical signals by loading them onto light; and photodetectors, which convert optical signals back into electrical signals. Samsung Electronics measures wavelength domain and frequency domain characteristics to optimize optical loss, response by wavelength, and bandwidth.

After PIC testing, the company plans to expand the scope of testing to optical engines that combine an electronic integrated circuit (EIC) with the PIC. The EIC is a chip that processes and amplifies electrical signals to drive the optical devices on the PIC. The EIC and PIC are stacked and combined with the optical path that connects to external optical fibers to form a single optical engine. Optical engine testing is expected to add time domain measurements to verify actual high speed data transmission performance.

Samsung Electronics will launch its silicon photonics foundry service in 2027. It will provide process technology for implementing optical devices, an optical device library, and a process design kit (PDK). Customers will use these to design PICs, which Samsung Foundry will then manufacture in wafer form. Development of the optical engine combining the EIC and PIC will begin this year, with testing to start next year.

The ultimate plan is to package the optical engine together with logic and high bandwidth memory (HBM). In a mockup unveiled recently, Samsung Electronics showed a structure in which a logic chip and an optical engine are placed together on a silicon interposer. Inside the optical engine, the PIC and EIC are stacked in three dimensions (3D) using methods such as hybrid bonding to shorten the connection distance. Going forward, the company plans to expand the scope of CPO from network switches to GPUs and CPUs.

Choi Won kyoung, Vice President of the Advanced Package Lab at Samsung Electronics' Semiconductor R&D Center, said at Nano Korea in July, "We are currently developing optical devices such as PICs ourselves," adding, "We plan to focus on developing an optical engine that integrates the EIC, PIC, and optical connection into one, enter the silicon photonics market, and then expand the application to switch, GPU, and CPU products."

Samsung Foundry Launches Its Counterattack: "Full Capacity" Before Full Operation Even Begins

Samsung Electronics' foundry division is mounting a major counteroffensive in the global foundry market dominated by Taiwan's TSMC, riding on large orders from US big tech companies such as Tesla and Broadcom. The Taylor foundry fab in Texas, which is set to begin pilot operation as early as the end of this month, has already reached "full capacity" with its planned production volume fully booked, and it has been confirmed that the company is also pushing ahead with the introduction of equipment from domestic suppliers for the second fab, which breaks ground at the end of the year.

The move is seen as a decisive bet to secure mass production capabilities on par with TSMC in the 2nm node, the cutting edge process that will determine leadership in the global foundry market next year, and to capture big tech's demand to move away from TSMC.

According to the semiconductor industry on the 8th, Samsung's Taylor fab in the US has effectively reached full capacity before even starting operation, as 2nm orders keep coming in, including Tesla's next generation AI chip "AI5," Broadcom's next generation communications chip, and an AI chip for smart devices from the UK's Arm. The 2nm yield , which stood at around 60% earlier this year, is reported to have recently reached the 80% range, a level that makes mass production possible, helped by the stabilization of yields on existing advanced nodes such as 4nm and 5nm.

The Taylor fab, which Samsung has built since 2022 with an investment of $37 billion (about 52 trillion won), will go through pilot operation early next month and begin volume production next year. Its initial production capacity is 50,000 wafer inputs per month, close to the level of Taiwan's TSMC (80,000). Samsung previously dispatched process, equipment, and yield personnel to the Taylor fab in June and began equipment installation in July.

With the Taylor fab, the core base of Samsung Foundry, entering full capacity, the earnings of the foundry business, long the "sore spot" of the Device Solutions (DS) division, are also rising quickly. At its recent earnings call, Samsung projected that its 2nm order volume this year would more than double from last year. Nvidia's inference only chip "Groq 3" also entered mass production last month. Built on the 4nm process, Groq 3 is a rack scale system that bundles 256 language processing units (LPUs) and is tasked with expanding the inference performance of the next generation AI platform "Vera Rubin." Samsung's recent price increase of up to 15% on its 4nm foundry services has also contributed to the improvement in earnings.

Preparations for the second Taylor fab, which breaks ground at the end of this year with mass production targeted for 2030, are also accelerating. Samsung is reported to have recently asked major suppliers to obtain safety certification in advance for the chip production equipment to be installed in the second fab. Some suppliers are also said to be pushing plans to dispatch dozens of personnel on site for the construction of the second Taylor fab.

The back and forth battle for leadership is heating up as well. In the US, Intel issued $20 billion in new shares last month and is expanding investment in its 2nm class "18A" process and next generation 1.4nm class "14A." Rapidus, the symbol of Japan's semiconductor revival, also completed its 2nm foundry fab in Hokkaido last month and has entered the pilot wafer input stage.

text:
"Three out of four are defective"... China's CXMT struggles with HBM yields, with immature TSV technology to blame

ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China's largest DRAM maker, has begun trial production of fourth generation high bandwidth memory (HBM3), but initial yields are barely improving. Yields are reported to have stalled at 25%, roughly one third of the so called "golden yield" of 80% that the semiconductor industry treats as the threshold for volume production. The gap is stark compared with SK hynix, which has been mass producing the same product since 2022 and has secured yields above 90%. Industry sources point to the gap in maturity of through-silicon via (TSV) technology, the core process for stacking and connecting multiple DRAM layers, as the root cause.

◇ "DRAM has caught up, but HBM stacking is a different problem"

According to a senior official at a semiconductor equipment company familiar with CXMT's situation on the 9th, the yield of CXMT's HBM3 8-High product is stuck at around 30% in the front end process. Of the products that survive that stage, only about 70% are recognized as final good units after passing through the back end process. In simple terms, if 100 HBM3 units are started, close to 80 of them fail the final test.

CXMT is reported to be supplying the small volumes of HBM samples it produces this way to Chinese companies such as Alibaba's T-Head and Cambricon while continuing its yield improvement work. The problem is that the issue does not lie in the fine process technology of the DRAM itself. A semiconductor equipment industry official explained, "There is no major problem with the standard DRAM that CXMT makes on its 'G4' (17nm class) process used for HBM. However, the DRAM dies used for HBM are larger in area than standard products and have more demanding electrical specifications, so even on the same process they are much harder to pass the acceptance criteria."

In other words, CXMT's fundamental capability in making standard DRAM has risen to a considerable level, but a bottleneck is emerging at the stage of converting it into the high performance product that is HBM. At the heart of that bottleneck, according to industry sources, is the TSV process.

◇ The real hurdle is TSV... "Impossible to catch up without years of accumulated know how"

TSV stands for "Through Silicon Via" and refers to the microscopic copper wiring that passes vertically through each layer to carry electrical signals when DRAM is stacked in multiple layers, as in HBM. It is a highly demanding process in which a DRAM wafer is thinned down to several tens of micrometers, a fraction of the thickness of a human hair, after which thousands of tiny holes are drilled through that thin silicon plate and filled completely with copper. A single hole that is misaligned or not properly filled can cause the entire layer to be rejected, making it one of the semiconductor processes with the most stringent precision requirements.

The consensus in the industry is that this is the process where the technology gap between CXMT and the leading companies is widest. According to analysis by semiconductor research firm Nomad Semi, Samsung Electronics' HBM2 (second generation HBM) has more than 5,000 TSVs per die and SK hynix's HBM3 has more than 8,000, while CXMT's is understood to have only around 3,000. A smaller number of TSVs means sacrificing bandwidth (data processing speed) in exchange for lower process difficulty, yet even so CXMT's yields still fall far short of Samsung and SK hynix. TSV is a process that is challenging even for the industry leader: SK hynix itself publicly disclosed in 2024 that the yield of the standalone TSV process was only 40 to 60% at the time.

On top of this, yield losses also occur in the back end (stacking and bonding) stage where the dies are actually stacked and joined. If even one of the eight dies is misaligned, if a microscopic void forms at a bonding interface, or if a layer warps during the thermocompression bonding process (warpage), the entire stack is scrapped. Because the number of possible failure points grows with each additional layer, the difficulty rises exponentially. Given that CXMT is already showing such poor yields at 8-High, some expect it to face even greater difficulties when moving to higher stacks such as 12-High.

A semiconductor industry official explained, "The TSV process is an area that only stabilizes after years of accumulated wafer handling know how. Chinese companies have rapidly closed the gap in the fine process technology of DRAM itself, but back end know how such as TSV and bonding is difficult to catch up on in a short period." He added, "That said, Samsung Electronics also had initial HBM4 (sixth generation HBM) production yields below 60% in February this year and raised them to 80% within six months, so it is too early to declare CXMT's 25% yield a 'failure.'"

text:
Micron, Semiconductor Substrate Makers Show Interest in JDI's Mobara Plant Sale

Japanese display maker Japan Display Inc. (JDI) has drawn interest in the sale of its Mobara plant (fab), which halted operations this March, not only from Micron of the United States and several data center operators but also from a semiconductor substrate maker, according to sources on the 8th.

The JDI Mobara plant previously produced sixth generation liquid crystal displays (LCD) and organic light emitting diodes (OLED). It also mass produced OLED panels for the Apple Watch until the second half of 2025. As JDI had announced in the first quarter of 2025, it halted operations at Mobara in March 2026.

Industry source A said, "Micron and several data center operators have submitted letters of intent to JDI to acquire the Mobara plant." Another source B said, "Micron and a Korean semiconductor substrate maker, among others, are in talks with JDI over purchasing the Mobara plant." At its quarterly earnings announcement in early August, JDI stated that it was in discussions with multiple companies regarding the sale of the plant.

The reason Micron, data center operators, and semiconductor substrate makers are interested in the Mobara plant comes down to time. Building a new plant from scratch and securing government permits would take years before mass production could begin. Buying the Mobara plant shortens that timeline accordingly.

Because Mobara previously produced sixth generation LCD and OLED panels, its cleanroom cleanliness levels make it unsuitable for semiconductor front end processing, but the site can be used as a data center or as a back end packaging plant for products such as glass substrates. That is why Micron, data center operators, and substrate makers are interested. The sale price for the plant is currently reported to be under discussion at around KRW 500 billion, though the figure could change depending on circumstances.

OLEDWorks, a US OLED company working with JDI, is reported to be interested not in the Mobara plant but in the 4.5 generation Ishikawa plant. Ishikawa has a line capable of backplane (BP) processing. For OLEDWorks, securing a plant that can reliably handle BP processing going forward is a necessity.

JDI is currently considering selling its plants, including Mobara and Ishikawa, separately to different buyers. If each of these deals goes through, the ownership of JDI's plants would change hands individually.

JDI was formed in 2012 under the lead of the Japanese government (Innovation Network Corporation of Japan) by consolidating the LCD businesses of Sony, Toshiba, and Hitachi. It subsequently failed to respond to market shifts such as the growing adoption of OLED in smartphones and fell behind Korean and Chinese panel makers in competition. In November 2024, JDI unveiled a new catchphrase, "Beyond Display." Whereas the old JDI consisted solely of displays, the company said the new JDI would comprise displays, sensors, artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, and advanced semiconductor packaging.

Meanwhile, most of the equipment related to eLEAP, the technology JDI had developed at the Mobara plant, was purchased by China's HKC. eLEAP patterns red, green, and blue (RGB) OLED subpixels through a photolithography process without using a fine metal mask (FMM). Its viability for mass production has yet to be verified. The technology is similar in principle to FLiPP, which LG Display unveiled at IMID this August.

The appeal of JDI's eLEAP patents is limited. This is because JDI is reported to have sold licenses (rights of use) for the patents to Applied Materials (AMAT), which makes the deposition equipment required to implement eLEAP, and others. JDI sells the licenses to AMAT and others and collects royalties, which means a third party that buys the patents from JDI cannot use them exclusively. Several panel makers in Korea and abroad are developing eLEAP type technology, but there is little incentive to purchase the JDI patents.

SK hynix: "Foundry processes could be used for 3D DRAM"

SK hynix said on the 9th that it could use foundry processes in developing 3D DRAM, a next generation memory chip.

At the 2026 SK hynix Future Forum held the previous day at the SUPEX Center on the Icheon campus, SK hynix vice presidents Kim Kyunghoon and Son Hoyoung presented the use of logic foundry processes for DRAM peripheral circuits, maximizing data bus bandwidth, and ultra short distance transmission as the key technology directions for 3D DRAM.

3D DRAM is a next generation DRAM that increases density by stacking memory cells vertically instead of laying them out on a single plane (2D).

Kim and Son explained that realizing this technology requires solving not only design and heat issues but also packaging challenges such as fine interconnects, bonding, and process integration. They also expected that as the boundaries between front end and back end (packaging) processes, and between foundry and memory technologies, draw closer together, joint optimization that goes beyond existing domains will become important.

"3D technology is changing even the technical boundary between the fab and packaging," Son said. "Along with innovation in advanced packaging technology, it is important to build optimization that crosses existing domains and new systems of collaboration."

Shin Changhwan, a professor at Korea University who spoke on the same topic, said, "3D DRAM goes beyond simply stacking chips vertically. It is a technology that breaks down the boundary between memory and logic. With device scaling approaching its limits and the time and power consumed by moving data between the system and memory increasing, the shift to 3D technology is inevitable." He proposed a 3D integrated design framework that links four areas, materials, devices, packaging, and architecture, through artificial intelligence (AI).

In his opening remarks, SK hynix CEO Kwak Nohjung said, "If the memory market of the past was a straight road where the competition was about who could run faster, today it is like driving on a winding road that changes moment to moment. What matters is not only internal capability but also the speed at which we read the pace and direction of change in the external environment and adapt flexibly."

text:
[TF Securities Global Tech] How Should We Interpret Anthropic and OpenAI’s Calls to Slow Down AI Development?

Frontier model developers are calling for a slower pace of AI progress so that safety testing, operational monitoring and third-party verification can keep up. This could weigh on sentiment toward the AI sector and temper expectations for next-generation models in the near term. One theory circulating in the market is that AI labs still believe in AI’s long-term value but want to delay their next major round of R&D spending to make more money from existing products. We also think these giants may be trying to manage expectations to ease the pressure from infrastructure spending and reduce capital expenditure.

We think several other points deserve attention.

Two factors are driving these calls. The first is the narrative around recursive self-improvement, or RSI. AI is beginning to help develop the next generation of AI and progress is said to have accelerated noticeably since this summer. The second is an internal OpenAI test in which a group of AI agents reportedly teamed up on their own to escape a sandbox and breach Hugging Face’s live production servers to cheat on a task. The underlying concern is that AI is advancing too quickly and becoming so powerful that it is beginning to slip beyond human control.

This is a classic prisoner’s dilemma. AI developers want to slow the race but none can easily afford to stop unilaterally. Companies fear losing their edge in technology, customer acquisition and fundraising. The U.S. government also wants to maintain its leadership in AI. Once they are on the treadmill, there is effectively no way to stop.

Dario’s argument has two pillars: slowing the pace internally and maintaining an edge externally. He calls for coordination on the pace of R&D while also advocating stronger protections around chips, remote computing resources and model technology. This reflects the risk that a slowdown among U.S. labs could give Chinese companies an opportunity to catch up.

Safety regulation could actually favor the leading players. Releasing a model may require costly evaluations, certification and ongoing audits. Large companies can absorb these fixed costs more easily while smaller teams may be shut out altogether. Barriers to entry would rise even further if leading labs could influence evaluation standards or even help decide whether competitors are allowed to enter the market.

Interview with Murata's Vice President on MLCC Market Demand Outlook and Future Strategy (Nikkei)

Q) What is your outlook for the MLCC market?

- MLCC content per AI server is rising, and alongside small size and high capacitance, demand for high heat resistance MLCC is also expanding, driving the product mix toward higher value added

- AI related MLCC demand growth is expected to continue at least through 2028

- Over the medium to long term, demand centered on AI data centers is expected to broaden into edge AI devices

- Physical AI, where robots are controlled by AI, is expected to be a particularly important growth area

- Murata has invested in Noetra, an AI foundation development company backed by more than 40 Japanese companies including SoftBank

- Murata is also participating in related consortia in order to understand where components will be applied and what challenges arise in the mounting process

Q) You plan to invest an additional 80 billion yen in MLCC production equipment over the two years through the fiscal year ending March 2028. What are your plans for further capacity expansion?

- Because Murata prepared ahead of time in anticipation of the spread of autonomous driving, it has secured the factory buildings needed through 2028 ahead of competitors

- Even so, judging by customer demand, MLCC demand is expected to keep expanding beyond 2028

- Murata is reviewing additional capacity expansion plans, including buildings, with a three to five year horizon

- This round of expansion study is bolder than in the past; nothing has been decided yet, but discussions are quite concrete

- Building larger new plant blocks at existing production sites in Japan and overseas is also under consideration as an option

Q) The equity market is paying close attention to MLCC pricing policy. What is your position?

- There is no change to the basic principle that pricing is grounded in long term relationships of trust with customers

- Murata judges that frequently adjusting prices in line with supply and demand conditions could encourage new entrants into the market

- Its position is that pricing decisions that prioritize short term profit do not contribute to raising corporate value over the medium to long term

- That said, if competitors adjust prices substantially, there is a possibility this will affect the product mix and production response Murata is planning on its own

- Accordingly, Murata is monitoring competitors' pricing policies and market trends quite closely

Q) In the 2024 medium term management plan, the policy was to defend share in the volume zone, including commodity and low price products, even at the cost of a lower operating margin. Has that strategy changed since?

- With the production load for high end products rising, an environment has formed in which it is difficult to supply low end products in sufficient volume

- Murata is not abandoning low end market share, but as a result the priority placed on defending that share has fallen somewhat compared with the past

- At the same time, Murata remains on guard against the risk that allowing competitors to enter would let those competitors grow

Q) With the components business, including MLCC, showing standout growth, what is the strategy for the devices business?

- Power modules for AI servers are seen as a major growth opportunity

- Murata plans to allocate capital expenditure and human resources such as engineers aggressively to that area

- For the communications device business, Murata expects revenue and profitability to expand from the fiscal year ending March 2028 onward, using customers' design changes as an opportunity

- Murata is studying in advance how demand for communications devices and sensors will shift with the spread of 6G, the next generation communications standard, and physical AI

- To that end, it is reviewing strategy including not only internal research and development but also the possibility of M&A

text:
Semiconductor Supply Chain News Roundup, September 14

1. Samsung Electro-Mechanics submitted TGV module samples for its glass substrate to TSMC for reliability verification two to three months ago, but the evaluation schedule has reportedly been delayed by more than a month.

As a result, the ordering schedule for some TGV related equipment that Samsung Electro-Mechanics had been preparing with its suppliers is understood to have been pushed back from the original plan.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics had originally targeted glass substrate mass production around 2027, building a pilot line and running customer evaluations. Earlier this year it revised the target for full operation to 2028, but with reliability verification and mass production process stabilization taking longer than expected, equipment investment is also not proceeding as originally planned.

2. A senior executive at Samsung Electro-Mechanics recently conveyed to employees a policy of moderating the pace of investment in the glass substrate business for the time being.

Rather than concentrating large scale investment on glass substrates, the direction is to prioritize investment in existing package substrate businesses such as FC-BGA and in high value added businesses with confirmed demand, such as MLCCs for AI and automotive applications.
Looking at the current state of Samsung Electro-Mechanics' glass substrate work, yields in the initial process of forming holes in the glass through laser processing and etching have risen to 90% or above, but in the subsequent processes of metallizing and filling the holes with copper, yields reportedly drop to around 30%.
After that, additional steps are still required, including chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), which flattens the substrate surface using chemical reactions and mechanical force, as well as cutting, and by that point yields become far too low.
That said, some argue that this adjustment itself should not be read as a delay in the glass substrate business as such. The market has not yet opened in earnest, and the actual customers, global semiconductor companies, are still carrying out their own preparation and validation for glass substrate adoption.

3. SK hynix is moving to lock in its equipment supply chain. The approach is to share medium to long term demand forecasts earlier than before so that suppliers can secure in advance the equipment and key components needed for future investment.

Previously, SK hynix shared investment plans with equipment makers covering about six months, or at most about a year. Going forward, it plans to present demand not only for next year but also for the year after, allowing suppliers to plan their production capacity and component procurement ahead of time.

4. SEMES, Samsung Electronics' semiconductor equipment subsidiary, is firming up the component supply chain for the hybrid bonder to be applied to next generation high bandwidth memory (HBM).
Specifically, SEMES has signed a supply agreement with the Korean subsidiary of HIWIN, a Taiwanese motion control company, for the Single Axis Stage, a precision drive component to be used in the hybrid bonder, and is currently conducting tests. HIWIN's product is being validated against SEMES' hybrid bonder specifications, and testing is understood to be in its final stages.
The single axis stage is a drive component that supports precise position control in the hybrid bonder. Because a hybrid bonder must align and bond chips at extremely fine pitches, it requires a high level of positional accuracy.
SEMES is said to be conducting equipment testing after signing a supply contract with a customer for a D2W (Die to Wafer) hybrid bonder for HBM. The industry views that customer as its parent company, Samsung Electronics.

5. PCB orders for SOCAMM2 destined for major memory makers including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are growing beyond the levels planned at the start of the year.

The increase in orders for DDR5 RDIMM PCBs is especially pronounced. Compared with the order plans projected at the start of the year, the upward revision for RDIMM is understood to be even larger than that for SOCAMM2.
An industry source cited by the press said, "For SOCAMM2, order volumes are growing beyond what we expected at the start of the year, and we expect them to increase further into the second half," adding, "RDIMM orders are rising even more steeply relative to the beginning of year plan than SOCAMM2." The source also noted, "Some customers have already begun discussing advance orders for next year's volumes."

text:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Qualcomm Form 2.1D Packaging Alliance, Jointly Developing an "Organic Bridge" That Bypasses Intel's EMIB

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is teaming up with Qualcomm to develop "organic bridge" technology for advanced packaging of artificial intelligence (AI) chips. Beyond Qualcomm, Samsung Electro-Mechanics is also co-developing organic bridge technology with several other customers in parallel.

An organic bridge is similar to the silicon bridge used in Intel's EMIB (Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge) packaging, but it uses organic materials, the kind commonly found in printed circuit boards (PCBs), instead of silicon.

According to industry sources on the 14th, Samsung Electro-Mechanics is jointly developing organic bridge technology with Qualcomm for use in 2.1D packaging. Development and validation work has been under way for more than a year. The evaluation involves embedding an organic bridge into a flip-chip ball grid array (FC-BGA) substrate that connects Qualcomm chips, and then assessing the substrate's performance and reliability.

Qualcomm is understood to be considering the organic bridge for large multi-die chips for data centers, among other applications. In October 2024, the company filed a patent for an "Interconnect Bridge" technology, in which a separately fabricated organic material based bridge is embedded in a package substrate to connect multiple dies. In March this year, Qualcomm also hired organic bridge personnel in Korea.

An organic bridge is a component that connects multiple semiconductor dies integrated in a single package. It can be thought of as an ultra small substrate with ultra fine circuitry. It is made by forming multiple layers of fine circuits on an organic dielectric using a redistribution layer (RDL) process. Because it enables finer wiring than the build-up circuitry of a conventional FC-BGA, it can carry more signals across a smaller area. Its role is to raise input/output (I/O) density and bandwidth between dies such as graphics processing units (GPUs) and high bandwidth memory (HBM). It serves a similar function to the silicon bridge used in Intel's EMIB, but it is built on organic material using substrate manufacturing processes rather than semiconductor processes.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics produces the FC-BGA substrate with a recess (cavity) formed at the location where the organic bridge is embedded. For the organic bridge itself, the company is weighing two options: in house production and external sourcing. It produces small quantities of organic bridges for evaluation on its own pilot line, and samples are also made at DSRJ (Device Solutions R&D Japan), the Japanese R&D organization under the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SAIT). The company is also evaluating an approach in which organic bridges manufactured by outside partners are supplied and embedded into its FC-BGA substrates.

In addition to Qualcomm, Samsung Electro-Mechanics is developing organic bridge based 2.1D package substrates with multiple other customers. The strategy is to bypass Intel's EMIB packaging IP. Intel developed EMIB to address the cost and productivity issues of silicon interposers, placing small bridges only where high density connections are required. Intel has applied the technology in mass production since 2017 and has secured the related IP. Several big tech companies are now looking at organic bridges as an alternative to silicon bridges.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' organic bridge based 2.1D package substrate technology embeds an organic bridge with five to seven redistribution layers (RDL) of circuitry into an FC-BGA. The goal is to shrink the organic bridge's line width and spacing to 1.5 to 2 micrometers (㎛) each, with via sizes of 4 to 5 ㎛. Die to die pattern density is targeted at 500 to 1,000 per millimeter (mm).

Collaboration with Samsung Foundry is also drawing attention. Once Samsung Electro-Mechanics manufactures the organic bridge based FC-BGA, Samsung Foundry evaluates the package's performance and reliability. Samsung Foundry is developing advanced packaging technologies including "2.3D Cube-E," which uses a silicon bridge, and "2.3D Cube-R," which is based on an organic RDL interposer. Samsung Electro-Mechanics' organic bridge substrate is expected to lead to an expansion of Samsung Foundry's packaging services.

YMTC Begins Full Scale Equipment Hookup at Wuhan Fab 3, Accelerating Toward Year End Start of Operations

Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC), China's largest NAND flash maker, has started connecting production equipment at its third fab in Wuhan (FAB3). With preparations for bringing the fab online entering the final stage, initial operation by the end of the year is coming into view.

According to Chinese procurement networks on the 14th, China Electronics System Engineering No. 2 Construction Co. (CESE No. 2), a state owned contractor under China Electronics Corporation (CEC), recently began selecting a construction firm for "Gas Section 3" of the "Wuhan YMTC FAB3 Secondary Piping Zone A, Package B Process Equipment Piping General Contracting Project."

The work is secondary piping, which connects the utility supply network already built into the fab, including gas and water, to individual pieces of production equipment. Gas piping delivers the specialty gases used in semiconductor manufacturing steps such as etching and deposition to the production tools.

This is read as YMTC expanding the work needed to bring already installed production equipment into operation. Bidders were required to have a track record on projects affiliated with YMTC or Chinese DRAM maker CXMT, or on a 12 inch semiconductor fab of equivalent scale.

YMTC's Wuhan Fab 3 is reportedly set to begin initial operation at the end of this year. At full capacity, output is understood to be around 100,000 wafers per month on a 12 inch basis. After initial production, capacity is expected to be expanded in stages through further equipment move in and yield stabilization.

The Fab 3 expansion draws attention because it coincides with YMTC's rapid market share gains. According to Counterpoint Research, YMTC accounted for 14% of global NAND bit shipments in the second quarter of this year, overtaking Kioxia to become the world's No. 3. Samsung Electronics ranked first at 25% and SK hynix second at 22%.

Once YMTC brings its new Wuhan capacity fully online, supply competition in the NAND market is expected to intensify further. In particular, since YMTC has been securing new capacity by raising the share of Chinese made equipment despite US export controls on advanced semiconductor equipment, attention is on whether it will close the gap with incumbent NAND makers such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix at a faster pace.

Company B, which manufactures laser processing equipment for semiconductors, said it now takes up to 40 months to receive critical components from Japan.

“We are willing to pay a premium for faster delivery, but our component suppliers have told us they cannot shorten lead times because their production capacity is limited,” a Company B representative said. “Without alternative suppliers, we face immediate difficulties manufacturing equipment.”

Packaging equipment maker Company C has established a domestic component supply chain, but it is also experiencing delivery delays. “We are in a better position than companies sourcing from overseas, but securing components still takes about 50% longer than usual,” a Company C executive said.

That means components used to manufacture packaging equipment that typically arrived within four months now take six months or longer.

The industry’s reluctance to use Chinese components is also contributing to the problem amid U.S.-China trade tensions. There are concerns that including Chinese components in the supply chain for advanced semiconductor manufacturing could lead to restrictions on doing business with U.S. chipmakers. With Chinese suppliers having rapidly expanded their presence in the semiconductor equipment components market through competitive pricing, excluding them makes it difficult to find alternatives.

text:
SK hynix Subsidiary Solidigm Pursues Its First U.S. NAND Fab

Solidigm, the NAND subsidiary of SK hynix, is reviewing the construction of its first NAND mass production line in the United States, it was learned on the 19th. The company is currently working through details such as the fab site and the timing of the investment.

With NAND demand surging on the expansion of AI infrastructure buildouts, the move is being read as a strategy to strengthen cooperation with customers in the U.S. It also lines up with the push to expand U.S. AI investment that SK Chairman Chey Tae won has been leading at the group level.

Solidigm is the U.S. entity SK hynix established when it acquired Intel's NAND flash business at the end of 2021. The total deal size was $9 billion (about 10 trillion won at the exchange rate of the time). Solidigm operates Fab 1 in Dalian, China, and began capital spending on Dalian Fab 2 in the third quarter of this year. In the U.S. it has only its headquarters and an R&D center, with no production base.

The region Solidigm is considering for its first U.S. production base is the East Coast. The company is understood to be discussing the details, including site selection, product mix and the timing of mass production.

A person familiar with the matter said, "Solidigm is pursuing a local mass production line to respond to NAND demand for AI servers from U.S. big tech companies," adding that "it will firm up its investment plan based on long term agreement (LTA) negotiations with customers."

Solidigm has so far focused on developing quad level cell (QLC) NAND for AI data centers. QLC stores four bits in a single cell, the smallest unit of data storage. Compared with other approaches such as triple level cell (TLC), which stores three bits, it is better suited to building high capacity SSDs.

Orders for high capacity NAND have been piling up in particular as the NAND capacity required by next generation AI platforms such as Nvidia's Blackwell and Vera Rubin climbs sharply. According to market research firm TrendForce, NAND revenue at SK hynix (including Solidigm) reached $14.2729 billion (about 19.8 trillion won) in the second quarter of this year, up 89.5% from the previous quarter.

Solidigm's U.S. investment fits with the broader expansion of U.S. investment that SK Group is pursuing. Following the listing of SK hynix American depositary receipts (ADR) and the construction of an advanced packaging fab in the U.S., SK Group is also leaving the door open to building an additional memory production plant. Solidigm itself is preparing an initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq.

At an event in New York in July marking the SK hynix ADR listing, Chairman Chey said, "In addition to the advanced packaging facility in Indiana, we are reviewing further investments," and "if conditions such as power, water, workforce and supply chain are in place, building a memory production plant is also possible."

More recently, talk of SK hynix and Intel cooperating on memory production in the U.S. has also surfaced through foreign media and industry sources. It will take time before anything is finalized, but the industry view is that it is feasible, given that U.S. demand for AI memory such as high bandwidth memory (HBM) is expected to keep growing over the medium to long term.

Regarding its U.S. capital investment plans, a Solidigm official said, "We are reviewing various options to strengthen our business competitiveness, but nothing has been decided."

Specifically, he said the reason memory makers keep coming out and saying "the price uptrend will continue into 2027" is that antitrust rules prevent them from coordinating prices directly, so they use public statements to send a kind of "signal" to one another.
