Chen also expects the cost of the SSDs and memory Acer holds in 2027 to be lower than this year. If that gets reflected in end product prices, he sees a possibility that prices at least stop rising and stabilize in the second half of next year.

Chen said prices could be raised further in 1Q27 as well. But since this is a period of pricing chaos, he expects the size of the increases to gradually shrink. He estimates component prices could peak around the middle of 2027, when the capacity that chipmakers have added is expected to start running in earnest.

After that, prices would enter a stable phase, and whether they can actually come down in the second half remains to be seen. He admitted, though, that nobody can know the exact timing of the reversal. Chen said PC selling prices coming back down is strictly "a hope."

He criticized component suppliers for treating price hikes like a fad. Countless suppliers are showing up to notify him of price increases, he said, and a whole series of components, from PCBs to glass fiber cloth to memory, are going up one after another.

He wrapped up by saying this chain of price hikes ultimately creates inflation, which in turn pushes central banks to raise rates, and that "this is not a normal phenomenon."

text:
Samsung Electronics to Double HBM4 and HBM4E Production Next Year

Samsung Electronics is expected to at least double its production of the HBM4 family next year compared with this year, including sixth generation high bandwidth memory (HBM4) and seventh generation HBM (HBM4E). This follows its plan to raise demand for "glass carriers," the glass supports that hold wafers while DRAM for HBM is thinned, to 2.5 times this year's level.

According to the semiconductor industry on the 20th, Samsung Electronics will increase its outsourced cleaning volume of glass carriers, which are essential to the HBM production process, from 20,000 units per month this year to 50,000 units per month next year. Only 10,000 glass carriers per month were needed last year, which means the volume doubles this year versus last year and rises 2.5 times next year versus this year.

A glass carrier is a support temporarily attached to the underside of a DRAM wafer for HBM to keep the wafer from warping or cracking while it is ground thin and holes are drilled through it. Because HBM must stack multiple DRAM dies within a limited thickness, wafer thinning technology and warpage control processes become more important as the stack count rises.

HBM4 and HBM4E, for which Samsung Electronics is especially preparing to expand production, center on high stack products of 12-High and above. The industry's analysis is that, even after accounting for the fact that glass carriers are reused after cleaning and that usage varies with how they are deployed at each process step and with yield, a 2.5 times increase in the related volume makes it highly likely that HBM4 and HBM4E production will be at least double this year's level.

In February this year, Samsung Electronics began mass production shipments of HBM4, which applies sixth generation 10nm class (1c) DRAM and a base die built on a 4 nanometer (nm, one billionth of a meter) process. In May, it also provided HBM4E 12-High samples to customers including Nvidia.

The industry expects Samsung Electronics' HBM production scale, measured by monthly average wafer input, to grow nearly 40% from about 180,000 wafers this year to about 250,000 wafers next year. In terms of shipment mix by product, some also forecast that the HBM4 family will rise from around 40% this year to about 80% next year as HBM4E mass production gets into full swing. An industry official explained, "As Samsung ramps up HBM production, it appears to be placing HBM4, a high value added product, at the center."

author: jukan05
text:
[Exclusive] SK hynix Begins Groundwork on Japan Fab

SK hynix has begun construction work for a memory semiconductor fab in Japan, just one month after the company said "nothing has been decided."

According to industry sources on the 28th, SK hynix has reportedly started groundwork for a semiconductor fab in Japan's Tohoku region. "It's unclear whether it will be a standalone fab or a joint venture with Kioxia, but it's true that foundation work is underway on site," an industry source said. "It shows how strongly SK hynix wants to enter the Japanese market."

The source added, "SK hynix has recently been asking domestic component suppliers to expand supply volumes. It's a sign the company is moving aggressively to respond to the memory supply shortage."

As recently as a month ago, SK hynix said a memory fab in Japan was "under review" and that "nothing specific has been decided." If true, the company moved at remarkable speed, beginning site preparation within a single month.

The Tohoku region is a major cluster for Japan's semiconductor and electronic components industries, with Iwate Prefecture at its core. Iwate hosts the Kitakami fab of Kioxia, a leading NAND flash maker, along with Japan Semiconductor, which makes microcontrollers (MCUs) and power MOSFETs, and Amkor Technology, which handles back end processing. Auto parts maker Denso and global chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron also have operations there. Adding the SK hynix memory fab now under construction would give the region a memory ecosystem spanning front end to back end processes.

This is also why Tohoku emerged as a leading candidate after SK Group Chairman Chey Tae Won said in August that the group was considering a joint memory fab in Japan. At the time, Chey said SK was "considering anywhere with abundant power and water," which further raised the odds of a move into Tohoku. Iwate in particular is known for excellent water infrastructure, given the concentration of semiconductor companies there.

If SK hynix builds a fab in Tohoku, Japan will complete a semiconductor triangle alongside TSMC in Kyushu and homegrown foundry Rapidus in Hokkaido, effectively linking the entire country through the semiconductor industry.

Meanwhile, SK hynix maintains that nothing has been decided yet. "The Japan memory fab is currently under review," a company official said. "Nothing has progressed beyond that."

text:
Samsung Speeds Up First P5 Mass Production Line, Pulls Equipment Installation Forward to Q2 Next Year

Samsung Electronics is moving faster to build the first mass production line (Ph1) at Pyeongtaek Campus 5 (P5). It was learned on the 28th that Samsung is discussing with major equipment suppliers a plan to pull the target for moving equipment into Ph1 forward from the third quarter of next year to the second quarter. The move is seen as reflecting Samsung's intent to secure capacity quickly as demand for high value DRAM and NAND for AI surges.

P5 is Samsung's next generation chip production base, targeted to begin operations in 2028. Construction of the Ph1 cleanroom began in the third quarter of this year. A cleanroom is the infrastructure that controls fine particle contamination, temperature, and humidity inside a fab.

Samsung originally planned to build the P5 Ph1 cleanroom early next year but pulled that schedule forward by about six months. Equipment installation for Ph1 was then set for around the third quarter of next year.

Recently, however, Samsung's P5 capex has picked up even more.

"Samsung has told us it will start moving equipment into P5 Ph1 around May or June next year instead of July or August as originally planned," one industry source said. "The schedule already changed once when the cleanroom was built early, and now investment is moving even faster."

Another source said, "Samsung is going so far as to ask for equipment to be delivered even in the first quarter of next year, saying it will store the tools somewhere else. Its commitment to investing early in P5 is very strong."

Discussions on P5 Ph2 investment are also taking shape. Ph1 is currently likely to be built as a DRAM and high bandwidth memory (HBM) line, and Ph2 as a leading edge NAND line, including 10th generation (V10) NAND.

"No formal purchase order (PO) has been issued yet, but Samsung is discussing plans with suppliers to build P5 Ph2 as a NAND line," said an equipment industry source. "Equipment lead times, the time from order to delivery, are very long right now, so Samsung is asking suppliers to secure related components in advance."

The main reason Samsung is moving up its capex timeline is the memory chip shortage. Global Big Tech companies are increasing orders for the high performance DRAM and NAND needed to build AI infrastructure, but memory makers including Samsung cannot meet all of that demand because of capacity limits.

On its second quarter earnings call in July, Samsung said, "Based on the demand we have received, demand that goes unmet this year is being pushed into next year, adding further supply pressure." It added, "We expect next year's supply shortage to be more severe than this year's, and the shortage to continue into 2028."

text:
Samsung's 2nm Foundry Yield Reportedly Nears 60% as It Goes All Out on Power Efficiency

Samsung Electronics' Foundry Business has reportedly raised the yield of its 2nm (SF2) process to close to 60% as it targets orders from big tech customers. Having moved past the yield stabilization phase, Samsung is said to be focusing its engineering resources on technical maturity, including performance per watt, through discussions with prospective customers. The company is determined to use next year's 2nm chip supply to Tesla as a springboard for winning more big tech customers in earnest.

2nm Yield Nears 60%, but Performance per Watt Is the Key

According to industry sources on the 29th, Samsung's SF2 yield has improved from the mid 50% range the market had previously estimated and has reportedly now reached around 60%. The market had estimated that yield, which was in the 30% range in mid last year, rose to the 50% range in January this year and to around 55% in August.

SF2 is Samsung's first generation 2nm process built on a gate all around (GAA) structure. Its first mass production product is Samsung's own mobile application processor (AP), the Exynos 2600. The Exynos 2600 is produced on the S3 line in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, and went into some Galaxy S26 series models earlier this year. For this chip, Samsung used a package structure that places a copper Heat Path Block (HPB) on top of the memory, which improved thermal resistance by 30%.

After launch, however, some overseas tests found that the Exynos 2600 used more power than Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon on the same workload, which drew criticism of its power efficiency. Some also saw this as a limitation of the process itself. To address this, Samsung is preparing its second generation 2nm process, SF2P, with mass production targeted for this year. Compared with SF2, SF2P reportedly delivers 12% higher performance, 25% lower power consumption and 8% smaller chip area.

With yield now on track, Samsung is said to be focusing on performance stability at the mass production stage. The company has reportedly put a large share of its engineering staff on making sure performance per watt, including heat and power consumption, does not vary once its chips are built into customer products. This is expected to support its case for technical reliability in future negotiations with large fabless (chip design) customers.

TSMC Alone at the Top, Samsung and Intel Fighting for Second

Intel, Samsung's competitor, is mass producing Panther Lake on its 2nm class 18A process at Fab 52 in Arizona. It is viewed as having achieved some success within its own product lineup, including a 56% share of the artificial intelligence (AI) PC market. However, 18A has yet to win any notable external foundry customers, and there is reportedly a view within Intel that it must stake its bid for external customers on the next generation 14A process (targeting mass production in 2027 or later).

TSMC is a step ahead of both companies after securing orders from big tech companies such as Apple. By absorbing existing customers such as Apple, AMD and Nvidia wholesale, it recorded a 72.5% share of the foundry (contract chip manufacturing) market as of Q2 this year, which widened its lead over Samsung Foundry (5.9%). 2nm wafer prices have settled at around $30,000, 50% higher than 3nm ($20,000), and TSMC has kept a "no discount" policy that offers no separate discounts even to large customers. The industry believes TSMC's 2nm capacity (CAPA) is booked through 2028.

As a result, observers expect a structure in which Samsung and Intel compete for second place behind a dominant TSMC. The prevailing view is that the timing of Samsung Foundry's return to profitability is tied to utilization at its Taylor fab. A semiconductor industry official said, "Yield approaching 60% and the start of work on improving performance per watt are meaningful signs of a rebound," but added, "The share gap with TSMC is so wide that it will take more time before this leads to any real change in the market structure."

text:
Was a good day to pick up more 
$SONY
 with a big hit to the stock today on Yen strength.

Overall, I do expect elevated volatility around Japanese net exporter stocks due to macro uncertainties for BOJ and the U.S. Fed.

Basically when the yen is weak, stocks like 
$SONY
 do better because they get paid mostly in dollars. When the yen is strong, stocks like 
$SONY
 do worse for the same reason.

BOJ is entering a hiking cycle, which means Japan's rates get closer to American ones. Every time that gap closes a little, the yen jumps and Japanese exporters sell off, and Sony's stock gets dragged along even though nothing about the thesis changed.

Sony guided ¥1.72T operating income assuming ¥153 to the dollar. The yen closed at ¥153 today. The move that hit the stock 4% just put the currency exactly where Sony said it would be. Profit impact versus guidance is zero, and that's on major sandbagged guidance, however, looks like some further strengthening on the yen is being priced in today based on a rumor about more BOJ hikes coming.

It's also a dual edged sword, Sony buys PS5 parts in dollars, so hardware gets cheaper. And if you own the ADR, a stronger yen partly cushions you, since Sony's yen earnings and yen share price both convert into more dollars.

None of it changes the thesis. GTA 6 revenue through the PlayStation Store mostly lands in dollars, euros and pounds no matter where the yen sits. FX moves the reported number by a few percent either way. The profit growth will far outstrip whatever the yen does to the translation line.

For me that means buying some more LEAPs on the drop, as the GTA 6 re-rating thesis is unchanged. My price targets unchanged.

text:
Something crazy is happening... 

With how indexes have performed amid $100 oil and rate hikes the market is maybe saying something it never has before.

Feels like investors are saying you're either in these stocks or just destined to watch your cash and bonds lose out to inflation.

If the 10-year is projecting inflation to rip, why would you want bonds that hardly outperform it? The Fed's hawkishness has done nothing to assuage these concerns because it's clear higher rates are not going to slow an economy this hot or solve a supply shock in energy. This is of course because higher rates don't end wars but also because the ROI on this technology investment is just that asymmetrical for the companies investing (a point Ackman made well).

Meanwhile this whole historical "risk-free" thing with bonds feels like it's falling apart. The U.S. Government is the least credible it's ever been. And higher borrowing costs from the Fed will make it harder to finance the growing debt due to reckless spending leading to money printing and then more inflation. 

At the same time large technology companies are the most credit worthy they've ever been. Even from a fixed income POV, I'd rather own corporate debt from 
$GOOG
, a business growing double digits with a phenomenal ROIC track record. The more capital a company like that can attract from investors who'd normally buy treasuries will lead it to then generate more return on investment and boost the stock as a result.

All of this points to equities continuing to rally. Debasement argument probably bullish for gold and BTC too.

author: michaelsikand
text:
After 
$MU
 earnings, it's clear the market believes the cycle won't peak in 2027 but is too fearful of the macro to award memory the multiple to match.

The stock is roughly flat after hours even after management said the pace of price hikes has peaked. 

While management says prices for memory will keep rising, they will do so at a "more moderate rate". Revenue and margins are still estimated to rise every quarter of 2027.

Memory stocks have always traded on rate of change, so it looks like the reaction reads as acceptance of a new framing around the industry.

That new framing? It's built on visibility we have never seen before in the sector. 

Customers have signed $150B in long term contracts with price floors, and these deals are expected to make up over 35% of Micron's revenue through 2030. At those floor prices, Micron expects margins above any peak memory cycle before it.

That's absolutley insane so let me repeat. 1/3 of Micron's revenue through 2030 is visible to us as investors at huge margins. It is extremely rare to have this level of long-term visibility into a business, especially one built on booms and busts.

While this is extremely bullish, the stock isn't moving because the entire AI trade is interconnected and investors are struggling to assess long term viability.

This visibility depends on the buyers of the memory being able to meet their commitments. Currently the macro picture is very bleak. Surging yields and rate hikes could make it harder for AI companies to keep buying memory, more and more of which is being paid for with debt. The Fed just hiked in September and the 10 year Treasury yield is hitting its highest level in 20+ years.

Overall, if the memory trade is to make its next leg up towards a more structural multiple, the macro picture must improve primarily with de-escalation in Iran.

author: octopusycc
text:
《深度和流动性对做美股夜盘的人有多重要？》

最近有个变化挺有意思。

最近身边几个长期做美股的朋友，开始越来越频繁地看币圈平台上的美股合约价格，把它们当成夜盘、盘前之外的另一个参考。

原因很现实：周末出了重大消息，判断已经有了，但美股不开盘。等到能交易的时候，价格可能已经跳过去了。

传统交易所也在拉长交易时间。NYSE Arca、Nasdaq 都在推进 23 小时、每周 5 天的交易安排，但周末依然留着空档。

币圈的美股永续合约把交易时间延长到了 7×24。不过对我来说，接下来要看的问题更实际：
这个价格，你到底吃不吃得到。

盘口有单、Spread 看起来不大，真碰上突发行情，稍微大一点的仓位进去，成交价可能完全是另一回事。

这也是我关注币安做这块的原因。它在加密市场积累的深度和流动性优势，如果能带给美股玩家，我觉得意义比单纯多上几十只股票大得多。

这件事有一些第三方数据可以参考。

CoinGlass 的 2026 年上半年报告里，币安衍生品成交量约 9.34 万亿美元，日均 OI 约 240.1 亿美元，在报告统计范围内都排第一。

更值得看的是盘口：BTC 合约在中间价 ±1% 范围内，币安的双边挂单深度约 2.36 亿美元，占五家样本的 44%，大约是第二名的 2.1 倍。

同一份报告里，币安 TradFi 永续合约上半年成交约 6663 亿美元，占五家样本的 55.5%。不过这个口径包括股票、ETF、商品和外汇，不能全部算成美股成交。

所以币安做这件事确实有底子，但 BTC 的深度不能直接当成美股合约的深度。具体到某个标的，尤其周末，我还是会看实际滑点、成交率，以及稍大一点的订单会把价格推走多少。

盘口看起来很深，也得下单的时候真能成交。

另外，这里交易的是永续合约，不是股票现货。资金费率、强平风险都要考虑，周末合约价格也不等于周一股票的开盘价。

对我来说，这些市场值得放进观察列表，有点像美股多了一个“第三交易时段”。

说到底，美股玩家不缺看价格的软件。

我们缺的是周末出了大新闻，有观点的时候能下单，而且成交成本别把这笔交易的空间吃完了。

 这张日线，从0.057美元附近走到0.1718美元，阶段高点已经是底部的约3倍。 

最近虽然有回调，但我更想知道：
这一段上涨之后，还有什么值得继续交易？

平时看 AI 股，绕不开 GPU 订单和 CapEx。设备还没开始赚钱，采购的钱谁先出？这次看 Falcon，恰好看到了它正在筹备的 GPU 远期融资产品，NEAR AI 提供未来算力购买需求支持。再加上已经上线的 Falcon Card，业务已经从链上收益往融资和支付延伸了。

但站在交易角度，最关键的问题还是：
这些业务，怎么给 
$FF
 带来需求？

按官方代币设计，$FF 的用途覆盖治理、质押奖励、USDf/sUSDf 收益加成和新产品优先参与权。Prime 质押进一步把180天锁仓和10倍治理投票权绑定起来。也就是说，持有和质押 ethereum:0xfa1c09fc8b491b6a4d3ff53a10cad29381b3f949，已经有对应的生态权益。

我看多的逻辑也在这里：如果生态真正吸引更多用户，这些权益就更有机会转化成持续的持币和锁仓需求。 这条传导需要真实使用来验证，不能直接把业务增长当成代币分红。

眼前还有一个催化：CLARITY Act 的程序投票，安排在美东9月15日下午2:15，也就是北京时间9月16日凌晨2:15。 这是推进法案的程序关口，还不等于最终立法通过。

Falcon 的机构数字美元 fUSD，已经由 Anchorage Digital Bank 发行，并接入 Ceffu，官方定位是面向 GENIUS 框架的“GENIUS-ready”产品。

如果 CLARITY 顺利推进、市场重新关注合规加密金融基础设施，Falcon 这条产品线就有机会获得更多关注，成为 
$FF
 的Catalyst。

所以，我对 
$FF
 后续偏多。产品还在往前走，代币有对应权益，接下来又有政策事件值得盯。比起盯着“已经涨了多少”，我更关注投票后的量价反应，以及回调有没有资金接。 投票若受阻，短线预期也要及时调整。

我现在越来越觉得，这轮市场真正的拐点，可能已经开始出现了。

过去几个月市场交易的是一条很简单的链条：

霍尔木兹受阻 → 原油高位 → 通胀重新抬头 → 全球央行被迫加息 → 风险资产承压。

但最近几天，这条链条开始出现了一股完全相反的力量。

美联储加息已经落地，日本央行也继续加息。

当高油价真的开始传导到通胀、利率和经济之后，美日韩对于原油问题的态度明显变得更紧迫。

美国持续释放战略石油储备，日本已经动用库存保障供应，韩国甚至开始讨论参与霍尔木兹海峡的航运安全。

更值得注意的是外交端。

中国和伊朗谈，核心议题之一就是尽快恢复霍尔木兹海峡通航；

美伊重新出现谈判窗口，伊朗甚至提出，如果美国缓和军事压力、解除港口封锁，可以在一周内重新开放霍尔木兹；

接下来的中美会谈，伊朗和能源问题同样绕不开。

所以我现在看这些事情，不会把它们拆开。

真正的拐点，不是哪一场和谈。

而是当高油价最终逼到通胀和加息这一步之后，各方第一次都有足够强的动力，让原油重新下来。

今天市场其实已经开始交易这股“反向力量”：

霍尔木兹缓和 → 原油回落 → 通胀预期降温 → 加息压力边际下降 → 风险资产重新获得支撑。

如果这个逻辑继续兑现，我认为接下来最值得交易的，可能已经不是继续追高原油，而是寻找这轮宏观拐点之后的反向机会。

author: ren_stocks
text:
I first reached 500% YTD back in May… and I felt invincible…

I had timed the market rally at the end of March and was investing in names that hadn't re-rated yet, most of the time using margin. For two months, 100% returns on stocks in under two weeks felt like the new normal, and AI compute demand was so high that nothing could stop it. Not the war with Iran, not rising yields, not the rising price of oil.

Yet the market always has a way of humbling us and keeping us honest. We all know what happened during the Korean unwind: a lot of people holding leveraged ETFs got liquidated… and my portfolio went through its biggest drawdown of the year. I clawed my way back above 500% by mid-August, only to get knocked down again, and it has taken until now to get back here, but I'm approaching it differently this time.

I'm using a tier system to hold myself accountable, so that most of my money sits in the highest-quality names of the AI buildout. I'm no longer using margin, I'm much more aware of the broader macro, and I'm even hedging for whatever may come my way. I'm not going to downplay the effort it took to climb back after the unwind, because it made me question even my own beliefs, and I think I'm a better, more rounded investor for it.

After everything that has happened, I can say one thing for certain: my biggest skill isn't being first or being the most bullish, but being adaptable and confident enough to follow through on what I believe will happen. I don't for one second think that 500% YTD is normal. It's the result of a lot of things going right and a lot of conviction in the direction we're headed.

I'm really blessed with everything that has happened in my life this year, and one of my main goals for the near future is to give back as much as possible to the community that has made me better. 

I'm still incredibly bullish on the AI buildout, more than I was a year ago, and I'll keep sharing my thoughts in the hope that my ideas and conviction help you understand it better.

Bullish, Ren

You're not bullish enough on interconnect. 

Jefferies latest report is just the latest example of how the BOM is shifting massively from the GPU toward memory and then interconnect.

In today's GB300 NVL72, the GPU is 62.5% of the rack and networking just 8.6%. By the Rubin Ultra NVL576 pod, the GPU falls to 46% and networking climbs to 22.4%, because once you link eight racks into a single 576-GPU domain, the interconnect between them becomes part of the computer itself. 

To put that in perspective, networking goes from roughly $5K per GPU in GB300 to about $21K in NVL576, more than 4x.

But getting the timeline right is the most important part if you want to ride each wave, and right now that wave is memory. 

Just look at Vera Rubin: it ramps from the second half of this year, and in Fubon's model it's the memory peak, with memory at a third of the rack thanks to HBM4, Vera's system memory and NAND. 

Rubin Ultra NVL576 lands in the second half of 2027, and that's where networking takes over: CPO debuts in H2 2027 and scales from there. But remember, the market looks 6 to 12 months ahead, so the interconnect trade starts well before then.

Memory and pluggables are the present, CPO is the future, and the rack tells us where the money goes.

Bullish

$NVTS
 

The US Army just picked Navitas for ALATTIS, a program to develop 10 kV silicon carbide power semiconductors, sponsored by the Army Research Laboratory.

The goal is to build a domestic manufacturing process for ultra-high-voltage SiC IGBTs that doesn't exist today, which says a lot about where Navitas' engineering sits, and it fits the same roadmap the company is pointing at solid-state transformers for AI data centers and grid storage.

That's the bridge to the AI trade: as racks move toward 800 V DC and megawatt scale, the conversion from the grid keeps moving to higher voltages, which is exactly where ultra-high-voltage SiC comes in. Navitas already works with Nvidia on the 800 V architecture for the Kyber racks behind Rubin Ultra.

This is a prototype development program with no dollar value disclosed, and 10 kV devices are still years away from real volume revenue. 

That timeline is the reason I sold 
$NVTS
 earlier this month, and this news doesn't change it.

Great validation for the tech, but for me it's still a wait-and-see name, so I'll keep watching from the sidelines.

Good news are always bullish

$NVDA
 
$NBIS


The biggest bear case on AI infrastructure has been that GPUs lose their value in two or three years, so everyone building data centers is overstating their earnings. This chart puts real prices on that argument.

Using Silicon Data's pricing, a six-year-old A100 still holds about 25% of its purchase price, which is where an accelerated depreciation schedule expects it to be at year two. An H100, four years after mass availability, is still worth 58%. And a B200 is trading at 158% of what it cost, a sign of how far demand is running ahead of supply.

That changes the math for everyone who owns compute. If a GPU is still worth more than half its price after four years, a five or six-year depreciation schedule starts to look conservative.

The neoclouds benefit the most, because GPUs are their collateral, their balance sheet and their product all at once, so every point of residual value makes financing cheaper and returns higher.

The honest caveat: it's Nvidia's own chart, the purchase prices are third-party estimates, and a B200 above 100% is a shortage price that won't last forever. But even the oldest chip on the chart is beating the bear case by four years.

Old compute keeps getting put back to work, and that's one of the strongest arguments for the whole buildout.

We are crushing the bears over here

author: ren_stocks
text:
$GOOGL
 

Most people don't know this, but in my retirement account, my biggest position by far is Google.

Alphabet owns more layers of the AI stack than any other company, and it's still priced like the search business everyone thought AI would kill.

Search grew 17% last quarter to $63.3B, so the "AI kills Google" story still hasn't shown up in the numbers. Below that sit Gemini and DeepMind at the model layer, then Google Cloud, which grew 82% to $24.8B while its operating margin jumped from 20.7% to 35.6% in a year. And at the bottom, Google designs its own chips, and it's now signing deals to supply multiple gigawatts of TPUs to other companies.

Cloud backlog reached $514B, up more than $50B in a single quarter, with just over half expected to turn into revenue within two years. That's roughly $257B already signed for the next 24 months, against a Cloud business running at about $99B a year today.

The price for all of it is about 22x forward earnings, below Microsoft at 25x, while growing faster. Ignore the 17x you'll see quoted everywhere, because it's inflated by a $98B gain on Alphabet's investment portfolio.

Capex guidance is now $195 to $205B for this year and set to rise significantly in 2027, and they raised $80B in equity in June to help pay for it, so you're buying a company that spends like a utility to grow like a startup.

It's hard to bet against a company this integrated across the whole stack. The one thing missing is a spark at the model layer, where Google has fallen behind OpenAI and Anthropic this year, and Gemini 4 might be exactly what lights it.

Bullish

The AI trade stopped being one trade, and that's the most bullish thing that could happen to it.

When multiples stop expanding, earnings have to do the work, and earnings are where this trade is strongest this Q. 
$MU
 just guided to $61.5B for a single quarter, lead times across the supply chain are still stretching, and semis trade at a discount to the S&P.

A market that moves together rewards being early, and we've had plenty of that over the last year.But that phase is mostly gone. 

A market that splits apart rewards knowing where the bottleneck is, layer by layer, and which companies get paid when it tightens. 

Not all companies are created equal, and we are seeing big dispersion between them.

A year ago the easy money was just owning the right theme. Now it goes to the right companies within each theme, and to knowing what sets them apart.
